claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2017-11-09 reports: The regional assessment identifies southern Belarusian Polesie, including the Polesie State Radioecological Reserve, as a climate-security hotspot where drought and flood risks threaten livelihoods, health and local economic security.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: The 2017 assessment frames short- and long-range human, economic and water security risks, not violent conflict or a quantified scenario-based conflict forecast.

claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2017-11-09 reports: The assessment says irregular monitoring in the most contaminated areas undermines timely warnings and prevention as floods, drought, dust and fires could spread Chornobyl radionuclides across Polesie.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: Conditional radionuclide-spread risk and monitoring weakness described in 2017; no current monitoring status or observed FCV mechanism.

gaps: General environmental, health and livelihood security is not automatically FCV evidence. No full climate-FCV pathway is assembled.
Reported sanctions-related data-sharing constraints are retained as attributed political/institutional context, without an unverified downstream adaptation outcome.

executive_assessment.text: Named evidence differentiates Grodno/Brest seasonal hydrology, Gomel/Pripyat water stress, Kopyl rural water access and a Brahin farm case.
Polesie evidence concerns interacting drought, floods, drained peatlands and radioactive-contamination risks. Its environmental-security framing is not a climate-caused violence finding.
Dated sector plans, peatland work and one supported farm illustrate reported capacities. Targets and institutional statements are not verified national adaptation or peace outcomes.
